theory.overview: Shor's algorithm (1994) provides an exponential speedup for integer factorization, threatening RSA encryption. While the best classical algorithm (General Number Field Sieve) requires sub-exponential time, Shor's algorithm runs in polynomial time O((log N)³). The algorithm reduces factoring to order-finding (period-finding) using modular exponentiation, then solves period-finding using the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT). A quantum computer with ~4000 logical qubits could break RSA-2048. This sparked massive interest in quantum computing and post-quantum cryptography.

sections.title: From Factoring to Period Finding
sections.content: Shor's key insight: factoring is equivalent to finding the period of a modular exponential function. For N = pq (product of primes), choose random a < N coprime to N. Consider f(x) = aˣ mod N. This function is periodic: f(x+r) = f(x) where r is the order of a modulo N. If we find r, and r is even, then a^(r/2) ≡ ±1 (mod N). If a^(r/2) ≢ -1, then gcd(a^(r/2) ± 1, N) gives factors of N. Finding the period classically requires exponential time, but quantum computers can find it efficiently using QFT.
steps: Pick random a < N, check gcd(a,N) = 1
Find period r of f(x) = aˣ mod N
If r is odd or a^(r/2) ≡ -1, try different a
Compute gcd(a^(r/2) ± 1, N) to get factors

sections.title: Modular Exponentiation
sections.content: The quantum circuit implements f(x) = aˣ mod N in superposition. We need a reversible circuit computing |x⟩|0⟩ → |x⟩|aˣ mod N⟩. Using repeated squaring, aˣ mod N can be computed with O(log x) multiplications. Each multiplication uses O((log N)²) gates with carry-save adders. The total gate count is O((log N)³), dominated by modular multiplication. The input register needs n = ⌈log₂ N⌉ qubits to represent x. The output register also needs n qubits for the result. This is the most resource-intensive part of Shor's algorithm.
sections.complexity: O((log N)³) gates for modular exponentiation
sections.resources: 2n qubits for input and output registers

sections.title: The Quantum Fourier Transform
sections.content: The QFT is the quantum analog of the discrete Fourier transform. On n qubits, QFT maps $|j\rangle \rightarrow \frac{1}{\\sqrt{2^n}}\\sum_{k=0}^{2^n-1} e^{2\\pi i j k / 2^n}|k\rangle$. It can be implemented with O(n²) gates—exponentially faster than classical FFT's O(n2ⁿ). The QFT circuit uses Hadamard gates and controlled phase rotations. The rotation angles decrease exponentially: π, π/2, π/4, π/8, etc. The QFT reveals periodicity: if a state has period r, the QFT output shows peaks at multiples of 2ⁿ/r. Measuring gives an approximation to k·2ⁿ/r for random k, from which we can extract r using continued fractions.
sections.insight: QFT transforms periodicity in time domain to peaks in frequency domain

sections.title: Period Finding Algorithm
sections.content: To find the period r of f(x) = aˣ mod N: 1) Initialize input register to superposition of all x: $\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2^n}}\\sum_x |x\rangle|0\rangle$. 2) Apply modular exponentiation: $\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2^n}}\\sum_x |x\rangle|a^x \\mod N\rangle$. 3) Measure the output register, collapsing input to superposition of x with the same f(x): $\frac{1}{\\sqrt{M}}\\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}|x_0 + jr\rangle$. 4) Apply QFT to input register, creating peaks at multiples of 2ⁿ/r. 5) Measure to get an approximation of k·2ⁿ/r. 6) Use continued fractions to recover r from this approximation.
sections.classicalPost: Continued fractions to find r from measurement

sections.title: Resource Requirements
sections.content: Breaking RSA-2048 (N ≈ 2²⁰⁴⁸) requires significant resources. Original estimates: ~4000 logical qubits and ~10¹² gates. Error correction overhead increases this substantially—physical qubit estimates range from millions to billions depending on error rates. Recent optimizations reduce requirements: using fast modular multiplication, optimizing QFT implementations, and better error-correcting codes. The race is on between building fault-tolerant quantum computers and deploying post-quantum cryptography (lattice-based, hash-based, code-based schemes that resist quantum attacks).

keyConcepts.name: Period-Finding to Factoring
keyConcepts.description: The mathematical reduction that makes Shor's algorithm work. Finding periods of modular exponentiation is sufficient to factor integers.
keyConcepts.math: If a^r ≡ 1 (mod N) and r is even, then gcd(a^(r/2) ± 1, N) often gives factors

keyConcepts.name: Quantum Parallelism + Interference
keyConcepts.description: Evaluate f(x) for all x simultaneously, then use QFT to interfere paths constructively only when x values share the same remainder pattern.
keyConcepts.analogy: Like finding the pitch of a tone by listening to its harmonics

keyConcepts.name: Phase Estimation
keyConcepts.description: Shor's algorithm is a specific case of quantum phase estimation—finding eigenvalues of unitary operators.
keyConcepts.connection: Modular exponentiation is a unitary; its eigenvalues encode the period

keyConcepts.name: Post-Quantum Cryptography
keyConcepts.description: Cryptographic schemes designed to resist quantum attacks. NIST has standardized lattice-based algorithms (CRYSTALS-Kyber, -Dilithium).
keyConcepts.status: New standards being deployed as quantum threat grows

complexity.timeComplexity: O((log N)³) quantum gates, polynomial in number of bits
complexity.classicalComparison: Exponential speedup over GNFS's sub-exponential time

steps.title: Classical Preprocessing
steps.description: Check if N is even, prime, or a prime power. If so, factor classically. Otherwise, pick random a < N with gcd(a,N) = 1.

steps.title: Initialize Registers
steps.description: Create superposition in input register (n qubits) and set output register (n qubits) to |0⟩.

steps.title: Modular Exponentiation
steps.description: Apply U_f: |x⟩|y⟩ → |x⟩|y ⊕ aˣ mod N⟩. This computes f(x) in superposition.

steps.title: Measure Output Register
steps.description: Measure output, getting some value y = a^(x₀) mod N. Input collapses to superposition of all x with that output value.

steps.title: Apply QFT
steps.description: Apply Quantum Fourier Transform to input register, converting periodicity to peaks in frequency domain.

steps.title: Measure and Extract Period
steps.description: Measure to get approximation c ≈ k·2ⁿ/r. Use continued fractions to recover r from c/2ⁿ.

steps.title: Find Factors
steps.description: If r is even and a^(r/2) ≢ -1 (mod N), compute gcd(a^(r/2) ± 1, N) to get factors.

practiceProblems.title: Period Finding
practiceProblems.description: For N = 15, a = 2, find the period of 2ˣ mod 15.
practiceProblems.explanation: 2¹=2, 2²=4, 2³=8, 2⁴=16≡1 (mod 15). The period is 4. Then 2²=4, and gcd(4±1,15) = gcd(3,15)=3, gcd(5,15)=5. Factors found!
practiceProblems.hint: Compute powers until you get back to 1.

practiceProblems.title: QFT Speedup
practiceProblems.description: What's the gate complexity of QFT on n qubits?
practiceProblems.explanation: QFT requires O(n²) gates. Hadamard on each qubit (n gates) plus controlled rotations between pairs (n(n-1)/2 gates). This is exponentially faster than classical FFT which needs O(n2ⁿ) operations.
practiceProblems.hint: Count Hadamards (n) plus controlled phases (n choose 2).

practiceProblems.title: Shor's Complexity
practiceProblems.description: What is the time complexity of Shor's algorithm for factoring an n-bit number?
practiceProblems.explanation: Shor's algorithm runs in O(n³) where n = log N is the number of bits. This is dominated by modular exponentiation requiring O((log N)³) gates. This is polynomial vs. sub-exponential for classical algorithms.
practiceProblems.hint: The bottleneck is modular exponentiation with O((log N)³) gates.

practiceProblems.title: Continued Fractions
practiceProblems.description: After QFT, you measure c where c/2ⁿ ≈ k/r. If c/2ⁿ = 0.375 = 3/8, what could r be?
practiceProblems.explanation: c/2ⁿ = 3/8 could mean k=3, r=8 or k=1, r=8/3 (not integer) or other combinations. We need to test candidates: r=8 is valid. Also k=3, r=8 is one solution. Generally, we test denominators of convergents from continued fraction expansion.
practiceProblems.hint: 3/8 is already in lowest terms. r could be 8 or a divisor if k shares factors with 8.

codeExample.python:
import numpy as np
from math import gcd

def modular_exp(a, x, N):
    """Compute a^x mod N efficiently"""
    result = 1
    a = a % N
    while x > 0:
        if x & 1:
            result = (result * a) % N
        a = (a * a) % N
        x >>= 1
    return result

def find_period_classical(a, N):
    """Classical period finding (for small N)"""
    x = 1
    power = a % N
    while power != 1:
        power = (power * a) % N
        x += 1
    return x

def shor_classical_simulation(N, max_attempts=10):
    """Classical simulation of Shor's algorithm steps"""
    print(f'Attempting to factor N = {N}')
    
    for attempt in range(max_attempts):
        # Step 1: Pick random a
        a = np.random.randint(2, N)
        g = gcd(a, N)
        
        if g > 1:
            print(f'Lucky guess! a = {a} shares factor {g} with N')
            return g, N // g
        
        # Step 2-3: Find period (classical for small N)
        r = find_period_classical(a, N)
        print(f'Attempt {attempt + 1}: a = {a}, period r = {r}')
        
        # Step 4: Check if period is useful
        if r % 2 != 0:
            print(f'  r is odd, trying different a')
            continue
        
        a_half = modular_exp(a, r // 2, N)
        if a_half == N - 1:
            print(f'  a^(r/2) ≡ -1, trivial root, trying different a')
            continue
        
        # Step 5: Compute factors
        p = gcd(a_half - 1, N)
        q = gcd(a_half + 1, N)
        
        if p > 1 and p < N:
            print(f'  Success! Factors: {p} × {q} = {N}')
            return p, q
    
    return None

# Test with small example
N = 15
result = shor_classical_simulation(N)

# Demonstrate QFT matrix
def qft_matrix(n):
    N = 2**n
    omega = np.exp(2j * np.pi / N)
    return np.array([[omega**(j*k) for k in range(N)] for j in range(N)]) / np.sqrt(N)

print('\n--- QFT Matrix (n=2) ---')
QFT2 = qft_matrix(2)
print(QFT2.round(4))

import Quipper

-- Simplified Shor's algorithm components

-- QFT on n qubits
qft :: [Qubit] -> Circ [Qubit]
qft qubits = do
  qubits <- qftRecursive qubits
  return (reverse qubits)  -- Reverse for standard output

qftRecursive :: [Qubit] -> Circ [Qubit]
qftRecursive [] = return []
qftRecursive (q:qs) = do
  q <- hadamard q
  q <- applyControlledPhases q qs 0
  qs <- qftRecursive qs
  return (q:qs)

applyControlledPhases :: Qubit -> [Qubit] -> Int -> Circ Qubit
applyControlledPhases q [] _ = return q
applyControlledPhases q (c:cs) i = do
  -- Apply controlled R_(2^(i+2)) rotation
  let angle = 2 * pi / (2^(i+2))
  (c, q) <- controlled_R c q angle
  applyControlledPhases q cs (i+1)
